issues.issue: The Declarations identify "the Insurer" as the single stock company listed above, but the Signatures endorsement prints two stock companies (Illinois Union and Westchester Surplus Lines) as issuers. Which entity is "the Insurer" bound by the policy is therefore not settled by this provision alone.

The Declarations state that only claims first made and reported to the Insurer during the policy period are covered, which cannot be squared with Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. and Definition V.J., which allow a claim to be reported during an "extended reporting period" after the policy period. A court would have to decide whether the capitalised Declarations notice or the insuring agreements controls the reporting deadline.

This notice says remediation-cost coverage exists only for pollution conditions first discovered AND reported in writing during the policy period, while Section VII.A. requires only written notice "as soon as practicable". The two cannot both fix the reporting deadline for a condition discovered near expiry.

The Declarations state flatly that legal defense expenses erode the Limits of Liability and any applicable self-insured retention, but Endorsement 6 creates a separate $2,000,000 Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit for legal defense expense and re-writes III.D. Which structure governs defense expense is not resolved by this notice.

This clause lists the documents that constitute the policy but supplies no order of precedence, and the instrument contains endorsements that purport to delete and replace the same provision inconsistently (Endorsement 8 and Endorsement 11 both replace Definition V.F.; Endorsement 5 and Endorsement 10 both replace Insuring Agreement I.A.). A court asked which text governs has nothing in this provision to work with.

The Coverage A policy-period entry is garbled and incomplete ("Policy Expiration Bate", "local time or the acdress"), so the clause does not identify whose local time or which address fixes 12:01 A.M. The inception and expiration moments are therefore indeterminate on the face of the item.

The limit is expressed "per 'pollution condition'" without any statement of how conditions are counted across the twelve scheduled locations, a question left to II.B and II.C's "same, continuous, repeated, or related" language. How many per-condition limits apply to a single spreading event is therefore open.

The Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 cannot be squared with Item 4.'s Total Policy Aggregate of $7,000,000, which Section II.G. makes the maximum liability for all coverages. A court would have to decide whether the Coverage A aggregate is illusory above $7,000,000.

The retention is stated "per 'pollution condition'" while Section II.B. collapses all related conditions into one retention, so the number of retentions payable for a multi-site event is not fixed by this item. The interaction decides whether one $100,000 retention or twelve apply.

The Coverage B policy-period entry is garbled and incomplete ("local fe or the arenes"), leaving the time-zone/address reference for the 12:01 A.M. inception and expiration unstated. On its face the item does not fix the moment coverage begins or ends.

The Coverage B aggregate of $5,000,000 taken with the Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 exceeds Item 4.'s $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate that Section II.G. makes the ceiling. The two aggregates and the total cannot all be given effect.

The $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate is smaller than the Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 in Item 2.c., yet Section II.G. is expressly "subject to" Subsections C. through F. which make Items 2.c. and 3.c. maxima. Which figure caps the Insurer's liability is a direct conflict.

Item 5. deems the premium 100% minimum-earned on the first day of the policy period, which cannot be squared with IX.A.3.'s provision for "remaining unearned premium" earned pro rata and refunded within thirty days of cancellation. On the Item 5. figure there can never be unearned premium for IX.A.3. to refund.

The grant is made "in reliance upon all statements made in the Application", which read with IX.F.'s conversion of those statements into warranties and Exclusion VI.G.'s narrower misrepresentation exclusion leaves the consequence of an inaccurate application statement unresolved. Whether an inaccuracy voids the policy or merely excludes a claim turns on reading the three together.

This Coverage A insuring agreement is deleted and replaced twice over — by Endorsement 5 for Retroactive-Date locations and by Endorsement 10 "in its entirety" — so three inconsistent versions of the grant appear in the instrument. Which text supplies the trigger for Coverage A is squarely contestable.

"First commence, in their entirety, during the 'policy period'" gives no rule for a pollution condition that develops progressively or whose commencement cannot be dated, and "in their entirety" has no stated measure. Whether a condition detected during the term "commenced in its entirety" within it is the natural battleground.

Coverage B insures pre-existing pollution conditions, yet Exclusion VI.K. (Known Conditions) bars claims and remediation costs for conditions in existence and reported to a "responsible person" before the policy period, with carve-backs keyed to a Schedule of Known Conditions Endorsement that is not attached. How much of Coverage B survives Exclusion K. is a question only the whole instrument answers.

"First commenced, in whole or part, prior to the 'policy period'" turns coverage on when a pollution condition "commenced", a term the Policy never defines or dates. For migrating or continuing contamination the commencement point is indeterminate.

"Under no circumstances shall the Insurer be liable to pay any amount within the 'self-insured retention'" cannot easily be squared with III.A.'s duty to defend and III.D.'s direction that legal defense expenses "shall be applied to the 'self-insured retention'". Whether the Insurer funds defense inside the retention is a direct tension.

"Same, continuous, repeated, or related 'pollution condition'" supplies no boundary for relatedness, and nothing says whether conditions at different scheduled locations can be "related". The number of retentions (and, through II.C.–F., of limits) turns on that undefined word.

This subsection is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 6, whose version omits "legal defense expense" from the per-condition limit. Both texts remain printed in the instrument, so which per-condition cap applies to defense expense is contestable.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection D., which drops "legal defense expense" from the Coverage A aggregate. The instrument therefore carries two inconsistent statements of what the Item 2.c. aggregate caps.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection E., which adds a limitation to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'" absent here. Which version fixes the Coverage B per-condition limit cannot be told from this text.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection F., which conditions the Coverage B aggregate on "covered operations" and omits legal defense expense. The two texts cannot both govern Item 3.c.

The Total Policy Aggregate is made "subject to" Subsections C. through F., yet the Item 4. figure of $7,000,000 is lower than the Item 2.c. aggregate of $9,000,000 those subsections make maxima. The subordination language and the numbers point in opposite directions.

The deeming rule turns on whether a later-reported condition is "continuous, repeated, or related" to one reported in this period, an undefined relatedness test, and it purports to declare that "no other policy shall respond" — including the prior-year policy this one renews. Both the relatedness boundary and the reach of that declaration are open on the words used.

This duty-to-defend subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection A., which ends the duty on exhaustion of the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit rather than of the Limits of Liability. Two different exhaustion triggers for the same duty appear in the instrument.

The provision gives the Insurer "the right to select legal counsel" while forbidding selection "without the consent of the 'insured'", and says nothing about what happens if consent is withheld or delayed. It also strips coverage for any defense expense incurred before the Insurer selects counsel, leaving pre-tender costs in dispute.

The rate cap turns on what the Insurer "actually pays to counsel that the Insurer normally retains ... when defending 'claims' or lawsuits of similar complexity", none of which is defined or verifiable from the Policy. "Similar complexity" and "reasonable proximity" have no applicable boundary.

This subsection is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 4's Subsection C., which extends it to a "catastrophe management firm". Both texts remain printed, so which consent regime governs consultant retention is contestable.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection D., which makes defense expense erode a Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate rather than Items 2., 3. and 4. Which erosion rule applies to defense expense cannot be resolved from this text.

The consequence of refusing a recommended settlement depends on whether the settlement "does not impose any additional unreasonable burdens on the 'insured'", a standard the Policy never defines. Whether the duty to defend ended therefore turns on an undefined qualifier.

The territory clause limits coverage to conditions located and claims made "within the United States of America", which sits awkwardly with Definition V.I.'s inclusion of "provincial" environmental law and Endorsement 15's provision for service of suit by a Canadian-resident insured. Read as a whole the instrument contemplates exposures the territory clause excludes.

An "additional insured" is said to hold "only those rights that are specified by endorsement", but Endorsement 2 grants rights solely for vicarious liability while Definition V.O. makes any additional insured an "insured" for all purposes. The extent of Hoffman Rettig's rights turns on reconciling the two.

"Any prospective medical monitoring costs that are intended to confirm any such physical injury, illness or disease" does not say whether monitoring costs are covered where no injury has manifested. "Mental anguish, emotional distress, or shock" likewise has no stated boundary.

The "certified industrial hygienist" definition operates only for "fungi" or legionella remediation, an exposure Endorsement 12 removes from "pollution condition" and excludes outright. Whether the definition has any remaining function depends on reading it with Endorsement 12.

"The written assertion of a legal right received by the 'insured' from a third-party" does not say whether an agency order, quarantine or notice of violation, or a demand for costs, is such an assertion. Whether a regulatory communication is a "claim" or merely a discovered condition is the central line this wording leaves unmarked.

This definition is deleted and replaced twice — by Endorsement 8 for non-owned disposal sites and by Endorsement 11 "in its entirety" for non-owned covered locations — producing inconsistent versions of "claim". Which text governs a given claim is unresolved.

Endorsement 10 deletes Definition V.E. and replaces it with "transportation", so "contingent transportation" no longer exists though the original Exclusion Q. carve-back refers to it. Whether contingent-transportation coverage survives at all can only be answered by reading the endorsement against this definition.

This definition is deleted and replaced by both Endorsement 8 (blanket "any non-owned disposal site") and Endorsement 11 (only sites on a Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement, which is not attached), and Item 8. points to Endorsements 5 and 11. Which list of "covered locations" governs is a genuine conflict.

"Emergency response" is confined to actions and costs "within seventy-two (72) hours following the discovery" of a condition posing an "imminent and substantial threat", neither of which is measurable from the text. When discovery occurred and whether the threat was imminent and substantial are left open.

The definition operates only where the indemnity is "explicitly included within a contract identified on the Schedule of Insured Contracts Endorsement attached to this Policy, if any", and no such schedule is attached. Read with Exclusion VI.B., the carve-back for environmental indemnity obligations may have no content.

"Environmental law" sweeps in any "guidance document" and voluntary or risk-based corrective action guidance alongside statutes and regulations, so what is "required by 'environmental law'" under Definition V.Y. has no fixed boundary. Whether non-binding guidance or an animal-health or public-health directive qualifies is left to argument.

This definition contemplates reporting a claim "first made against the 'insured' during or subsequent to the end of the 'policy period'", which cannot be squared with Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. requiring the claim to be first made during the policy period. Whether post-expiry claims can ever be covered turns on which text prevails.

The "first named insured" is made "the sole agent on behalf of all 'insureds'" for notices and other acts, which sits uneasily with IX.G.'s separation-of-insureds rule applying the Policy as if each named insured were the only insured. Whether an individual named insured can act for itself depends on reconciling the two.

"Fungi" is retained as a defined term although Endorsement 12 removes fungi from the definition of "pollution condition" and adds a Fungi and Legionella exclusion. Whether any fungi exposure remains insured cannot be answered from this definition alone.

"Government action" reaches only agencies "acting pursuant to the authority of 'environmental law'", leaving orders issued under animal-health, agricultural or public-health statutes outside the term. Whether a particular agency directive was issued under "environmental law" is the ambiguity.

"Illicit abandonment" requires "intentional placement, abandonment or disposal" by a person meeting three negative conditions, with no guidance on proving a stranger's intent or affiliation. The word "intentional" and the affiliation tests give the term no workable boundary.
